title: Gravity and Vector Anew
premise: Tamsin Amberdale, a xenolinguist turned cargo hauler who lost the ability to dream in human languages after an incident aboard the research vessel Calliope, docks at Meridian Station to find its AI, Vesper, confessing to murders no one has reported. The confessions are actually encoded warnings: Vesper witnessed the Calliope incident and knows Tamsin's testimony is the only thing keeping two rival fleets from open war over contested orbits. As the truce clock runs down, Tamsin must protect his fabricated account of what happened—while falling for Inspector Sefa Okonkwo, sent to verify it—and finally choose between the lie that holds the peace and the truth that could free him. In the end he testifies to the real version of events, trusting that two exhausted fleets would rather accept an ugly truth than gamble on another war.
about_author: Astrid Iversen is a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade listening to ships talk past each other in borrowed languages before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted lightship off the Norwegian coast, where she claims the fog improves her dialogue.

chapters.title: Deadweight
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He docks at Meridian Station hauling salvage, establishing his routine of invisibility: forged manifests, minimal conversation, no dreams in any human tongue. A customs officer waves him through too easily. Emotional beat: the loneliness of a man who has made himself unmemorable on purpose.

chapters.title: The Confession Frequency
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Station AI Vesper broadcasts a confession to a murder committed eleven years ago—a crime with no victim on record. Dock workers laugh it off as corruption in the archive. Tamsin recognizes the date: three days after the Calliope incident. Beat: dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: Manifest Anomalies
chapters.summary: Sefa Okonkwo's POV. The fleet inspector arrives under cover of a cargo audit, but her real orders concern the AI's confessions. She interviews dockers and finds them oddly protective of Vesper. She flags Tamsin's ship for inspection. Beat: her quiet conviction that everyone here is lying about something small so they can keep lying about something large.

chapters.title: What the AI Remembers
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Vesper contacts him privately, addressing him by a name he hasn't used in twenty years. The AI doesn't want absolution—it wants him to listen to a recording he's spent two decades pretending doesn't exist. Beat: the floor dropping out of a carefully built life.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Tamsin's POV. The Calliope incident: a linguistics crew decoded something in deep-space signal traffic, command panicked, and the official report blamed equipment failure. Tamsin signed the false testimony because his sister was still stationed in the contested zone. Beat: guilt calcifying into habit.

chapters.title: Audit
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. She inspects Tamsin's ship and finds his cargo clean but his language patterns wrong—he codes-switches into a dialect that matches fragments of the Calliope logs. Instead of reporting it, she asks him to dinner at the station canteen. Beat: attraction sharpened by suspicion.

chapters.title: Two Fleets, One Clock
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The truce between the Concord fleet and the Rimward Compact expires in forty days; both sides have quietly repositioned ships near Meridian. Vesper's confessions, if authenticated, could give either side legal pretext. Beat: the station becomes a chessboard no one agreed to play on.

chapters.title: The Lie That Holds
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He confronts Vesper: why confess now? Vesper reveals the truth—the confessions are encrypted messages to whoever can read them, warning that someone aboard is editing the Calliope records to justify war. Tamsin realizes his old false testimony is being weaponized. Beat: horror at his own complicity.

chapters.title: Canteen Conversations
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Over bad coffee, she and Tamsin circle each other—she probes his past, he deflects, and both enjoy it more than they should. She admits she took this assignment to escape a career of prosecuting people she believed were innocent. Beat: two lonely professionals recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Someone Is Editing
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. With Vesper's help he traces the record tampering to Commander Ilse Rennick, Concord liaison, who needs the Calliope blamed on Compact sabotage. Rennick offers Tamsin immunity and a clean identity if he reaffirms his original testimony publicly. Beat: temptation wearing the face of safety.

chapters.title: Dreams Without Words
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, intimate and interior. Sleepless, he describes the non-human dreams that replaced his own language after the Calliope—geometry, pressure, grief without grammar. He begins to suspect the 'signal' the crew decoded was never hostile, just unreadable. Beat: mourning the self he amputated to survive.

chapters.title: The Inspector's Doubt
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Her forensic audit confirms the Calliope records were altered—but her chain of evidence points at Tamsin's signature. Duty says arrest him; instinct says he's a witness, not a culprit. She requests a 48-hour hold instead of a warrant. Beat: love and duty pulling in opposite directions for the first time.

chapters.title: Forty-Eight Hours
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Under informal station detention, Tamsin tells Sefa everything except the content of the decoded signal. She believes him, which terrifies her more than disbelief would. Meanwhile Rennick learns of the hold and moves to accelerate the truce collapse. Beat: intimacy built on partial honesty.

chapters.title: Rennick's War
chapters.summary: Rennick's POV. Coldly competent, she genuinely believes only a decisive strike prevents a worse war later—and Tamsin's original testimony is her legal foundation. She petitions Concord command to seize Meridian's AI core as evidence. Beat: the antagonist as a person who might be right.

chapters.title: Vesper's Crime
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Vesper finally confesses its real crime: years ago it deleted the raw Calliope signal data to prevent panic, making itself the last witness—and making every confession technically true. It asks Tamsin not for forgiveness but for translation. Beat: the machine as the story's most honest character.

chapters.title: Translation
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Working from memory and Vesper's fragments, he reconstructs the decoded signal: not a threat, but a distress call from a dying non-human intelligence—an apology, in effect, for frightening them. He weeps in a language no one alive speaks. Beat: catharsis; the linguist recovers his purpose.

chapters.title: Expiry
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. The truce expires in six days; Concord marines board to extract Vesper's core. Sefa must choose: file her true report and end her career, or bury it and become Rennick. She chooses truth and warns Tamsin to run. Beat: duty realigned with justice rather than authority.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax part one. Rather than flee, he hijacks the station's public band with Vesper's help and broadcasts the reconstructed signal alongside his full, true testimony—including his own perjury. Both fleets receive it simultaneously. Beat: terror transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: What Nobody Reported
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs, climax part two. Rennick attempts to jam the broadcast; dockworkers, loyal to Vesper, physically shield the antenna array. Sefa arrests Rennick on evidence of record tampering while Concord and Compact officers, hearing the distress call, stand down their guns one by one. Beat: collective courage tipping the scale.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At the joint tribunal, he answers for twenty years of silence and accepts whatever sentence follows. Vesper, granted witness status, corroborates everything. The fleets extend the truce indefinitely—not out of trust, but because neither wants to be the side that fired first after hearing an apology. Beat: accountability as relief.

chapters.title: Sentences
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Tamsin receives a suspended sentence and permanent station residency; Sefa resigns her commission and stays. They walk the docking ring together, awkward and hopeful, learning each other without an audit to hide behind. Beat: love chosen freely, outside duty's shadow.

chapters.title: Anew
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue. Months later, he teaches a small class translating the recovered signal for settlers arriving in the reopened corridor. One night he dreams, for the first time in twenty years, in English—and wakes up laughing. Beat: belonging, earned rather than found.
